definition: Kevin Lynch's term for how easily a place forms a clear mental map in the people who use it.
Walt Disney's word for a tall visual magnet, such as a castle, that pulls guests through a space and anchors their sense of direction.
A junction or gathering point where paths meet and guests make a navigation decision.
A worn shortcut created by people repeatedly leaving the official path for a more direct route.
Helbing's crowd simulation in which each pedestrian is pulled toward a goal and pushed away from others and walls.
The curve relating crowd density to flow, which rises and then collapses as people pack too tightly to move.
Fruin's A-to-F grading of walkways, stairs and queues by how much space each person has.
Edward T. Hall's study of the personal-space distances people keep from one another.
The tendency to copy what other people are doing when unsure, such as joining a line because it is long.
The way options are arranged and defaulted, which steers decisions without removing any choice.
A design that predictably changes behaviour while leaving every option open, such as a default or an ordering.
Continuing to invest time or money because of what has already been spent rather than what lies ahead.
A procedure letting adults in a group take turns on a ride while one waits with a child who cannot ride.
Measured body dimensions from population surveys, used to size seats, restraints and reach limits.
Choosing the slice of a population, such as the 5th to 95th percentile, that a design must fit.
The seated width across the hips, the measurement that most often decides whether a guest fits a ride seat.
The design requirement, in standards such as ASTM F2291, that a restraint and seat keep the rider safely in the vehicle through all ride forces.
The noise exposure, 85 dBA averaged over eight hours in US rules, above which hearing protection and monitoring are required.
A ride seat positioned and shaped so a guest can slide across to it from a wheelchair.
Designing a space so the widest range of people can use it without special routes or exceptions.
A published rating of each attraction on sound, light, smell, touch and motion so guests can plan around sensory needs.
A low-stimulation space with dim lighting and soft seating where an overloaded guest can recover inside the park.
Adapting a ride or story for a new country by changing its meaning, characters and symbols, not just its language.
Slater's term for the sense of being in a place, produced by consistent sensory input that responds to your movement.
Slater's term for the sense that events are really happening, produced by a world that reacts to you and behaves consistently.
The state of being carried into a story so fully that attention, imagery and emotion all focus on it.
Mori's observation that almost-human figures provoke unease rather than the affection given to clearly stylised ones.
Janet Murray's term for the satisfying power to take meaningful action and see its results.
